name: Dogs Trust
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. people in the UK (behaviour-line owners, Freedom's survivors and their children, homeless owners: about 84%) and UK and Irish dogs (under 1%); fewer dog bites and overseas treatment, neutering and training (about 15%) spread over WVS's and the grantees' main countries by grant size (a judgment).
summary: Dogs Trust, the UK's largest dog welfare charity, rehomed about 10,000 dogs in the UK and Ireland in 2025, ran a behaviour support line and other prevention services, fostered dogs for people escaping domestic abuse, campaigned for the 2025 law against puppy smuggling, and through its sister charity Worldwide Veterinary Service treated and sterilised dogs overseas; this model covers all of that except rabies vaccination, which has its own model. At the site's defaults it comes to about 0.00005 years of healthy life per $1,000, far below the median animal charity because care for individual dogs reaches few animals per dollar: about $205m for a few hundred thousand days of a dog's disabling pain spared, most of them from neutering and treatment overseas, and at the default weight on animal suffering the dogs' days count less than the people the work also helps: owners given behaviour advice, survivors of domestic abuse (and their children) who could leave because Freedom kept their dog, and homeless owners (together most of the result, judgments), and fewer people bitten where neutering shrinks free-roaming populations (a side effect). The biggest uncertainties are the people's gains, how much a rehomed or neutered dog's life improves (our judgment, with no study measuring it), and the weight on animal suffering; every branch is discounted for missing data, and the model's own ranges together span more than a thousandfold, so the figure is mostly uncertainty.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

Dogs rehomed by Dogs Trust's centres, UK and Ireland, 2025

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.page: p. 87 (PDF page 44), financial report, our targets
source.quote: Dogs rehomed by our rehoming centres (UK and Ireland) 10,023 9,914

rows.explainer: Dogs placed in new homes in 2025, including 2,694 rehomed from foster care (p. 25) and 479 long-stay 'Underdogs'. The highlights (p. 22) give the same 10,023 for the UK alone and Dogs Trust Ireland reports 859 of its own (p. 36), so the total may be up to 10,882; we take the audited report's measure. 11,374 dogs were cared for in the UK centres.

rows.label: Rehoming: suffering averted per day of the dog's new life, in days of disabling pain
rows.explainer: Our judgment on Ambitious Impact's pain scale (disabling 1, hurtful 0.1, annoying 0.01). A dog that comes in has been given up (an owner who can no longer cope, often with behaviour or medical problems), found stray, or seized; its likely alternative is staying in that home, private resale online, or a stray kennel. In a screened home with vet care and behaviour support we put the difference at about two hours of hurtful-level distress a day (0.1 × 2/24 = 0.008) plus untreated illness, 0.01 days of disabling pain a day, from 0.003 (mostly settled dogs whose old home would have managed) to 0.03 (dogs with untreated medical or severe anxiety problems). No study measures it; anchor: shelter-welfare and relinquishment surveys (behaviour is the commonest reason dogs under three are put to sleep, p. 7). Days in kennels before rehoming are a cost we don't count separately; fostering (3,546 dogs) cuts them.

rows.label: Rehoming: years the dog's better life lasts

source.title: Teng et al. 2022, Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom, Scientific Reports 12:6415
source.quote: life expectancy at age 0 was 11.23 [95% confidence interval (CI): 11.19–11.27] years

rows.explainer: UK dogs live 11.23 years from birth (VetCompass, 30,563 dogs). Rehomed dogs are mostly young adults (a judgment: about 2 to 4 years old), leaving about 8 years, times the share that stay in their new home (most; some are returned): 7, from 4 (older dogs, more returns) to 9.

rows.label: Rehoming: days of disabling pain spared per dog, discounted
rows.explainer: Every future year discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Rehoming: days of pain spared before adjustments
Rehoming: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.7, the template's anchor for a judged welfare effect with no trial, 0.5 to 0.9: the per-day effect is our own reading of the welfare literature, not a measurement of these dogs.

rows.label: Rehoming: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Most dogs given up would still find some home: other rescues (though full), private rehoming and resale online, or the owner keeping them; and some would be put to sleep, which counts nothing either way here (deaths are not suffering). Adopters who would otherwise have bought a puppy also add to demand for breeding. Our judgment: 30% of the welfare difference is Dogs Trust's, 10% to 60%. Anchor: more than 47,000 people contacted Dogs Trust about giving up a dog in 2024 (its 2024 report) against about 10,000 places a year, so it is one of several routes.

rows.label: Rehoming: Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Volunteers (68,035 hours in 2025, p. 40) and 1,721 foster carers (p. 25) give unpaid time: about 70,000 hours plus roughly 200,000 foster hours (3,546 dogs × about four weeks × two hours a day, our judgment) at the UK National Living Wage of £12.21, about £3.3m beside £64.4m of spending, so 95%; 0.93 allows for adopters' own adoption costs beyond the fee. 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Rehoming: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Rehoming: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Some adoptions break down and the dog comes back (and is counted again when rehomed); 0.9, 0.8 to 1.

rows.label: Rehoming: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Dogs Trust counts the dogs but no controlled study measures how much less they suffer, so the effect is our judgment from the welfare literature.

rows.label: Prevention: dogs helped
rows.explainer: Dogs, not calls (19,857 calls to the line). A dog seen by two services counts twice; the overlap is unpublished and is in the delivery adjustment.

rows.label: Prevention: suffering averted per day, in days of disabling pain
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The line's commonest problems are separation-related behaviour (32%), reactivity to dogs (29%) and to people (19%) (p. 15): a dog with separation distress spends hours a day anxious (hurtful, 0.1). Two hours of hurtful distress a day removed in about a third of the dogs gives 0.1 × 2/24 / 3 ≈ 0.003 days of disabling pain a day; Dog School puppies mostly have no problem to fix (the low end, 0.0005), clinical cases more (0.01). Anchor: the rehoming judgment, scaled by the share of dogs with a problem the advice fixes. Relinquishment or euthanasia averted counts only through these days.

rows.label: Prevention: years the improvement lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment: behaviour problems managed, not cured, often return; two years, 0.5 to 5.

rows.label: Prevention: days of disabling pain spared per dog, discounted
Prevention: days of pain spared before adjustments
Prevention: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.6, below rehoming's 0.7: the only outcome data are users' satisfaction (97% would recommend the line, p. 15), owner-reported and uncontrolled. 0.4 to 0.8.

rows.label: Prevention: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Owners could pay a trainer or behaviourist, use free online advice, or the problem could ease with age. Our judgment 0.5, 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Prevention: Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Delivered by Dogs Trust staff; vets who refer clinical cases share a little. 0.9, 0.8 to 1. The owners' own time training the dog is not counted as another's resource, as for every programme's participants.

rows.label: Prevention: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Prevention: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Owners follow advice only in part, and some dogs are counted by more than one service: 0.7, 0.5 to 0.9.

rows.label: Prevention: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Dogs Trust counts the dogs but no controlled study measures how much less they suffer, so the effect is our judgment from the welfare literature.

rows.label: Prevention: all adjustments combined
Prevention: research and education, as a share of the branch's result
rows.explainer: The prevention line also pays £0.62m of research grants (Edinburgh, Liverpool, the RVC, note 7(b)) and education, moved online in 2025. Our judgment: 10% more than the advice's own result, 0 to 30%; research on dog welfare is cheap relative to its reach but its effect on dogs' days is unmeasured. A side effect, weighed by the shared slider.

Animals treated through WVS's veterinary care programmes, 2025

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: 158,647 animals were treated through veterinary care programmes

rows.explainer: Mostly free-roaming and owned dogs and cats in 26 countries; WVS also treats working equines and others.

rows.label: Treatment: days of disabling pain spared per animal treated
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a treated wound, mange, tick fever or fracture shortens weeks of hurtful pain (0.1 a day) to days; about a month of hurtful pain spared is 3 days of disabling pain, from 0.5 (minor treatments, deworming) to 15 (surgery that saves weeks of severe pain). Spread over weeks, so not discounted.

rows.label: Treatment: days of pain spared before adjustments
Treatment overseas: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: 4,907 veterinary professionals were trained

rows.label: Training: animals a year treated better because of the training, per person trained
rows.explainer: Our judgment: WVS says each vet trained helps thousands over a career (p. 33), but many trainees are already practising and the course changes a part of their work: 30 animals a year treated better (with less pain or a working treatment), 5 (short courses, few patients) to 150 (new surgeons in busy practice).

rows.label: Training: years the skill is used
rows.explainer: Our judgment: skills fade and people leave the work; 5 years, 2 to 15.

rows.label: Training: pain spared per better-treated animal, as a share of a WVS treatment's
rows.explainer: Our judgment: better care than they'd have had from the same vet untrained, not care against none: 30% of a WVS treatment's days (trt_pain_days_per_animal), 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Training: days of pain spared before adjustments
rows.formula: trn_vets_trained * trn_extra_animals_per_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, trn_years_in_practice) * trn_share_of_treatment_effect * trt_pain_days_per_animal
rows.explainer: Bosnia's ~500 vets trained over a decade and WVS's education of 5 million people aren't counted separately; their small yearly share is within these ranges.

rows.label: Training: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.6, below the care branches: no follow-up of trainees' practice is published; 0.4 if little of the training is used, 0.8 if close to right.

rows.label: Training: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Our judgment: some trainees would have learnt elsewhere (universities, other NGOs' courses); 0.7, 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Training: Dogs Trust's share of the resources
rows.explainer: As for treatment: training centres' partners and trainees' own time share the cost; 0.6, 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Training: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Training: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Some counted trainees attend only part of a course: 0.8, 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Training: counted less where the outcome isn't measured

Animals sterilised by WVS, 2025

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: 43,444 animals were sterilised to manage numbers humanely

rows.label: Sterilisations paid for by Dogs Trust's grants to overseas organisations, 2025
rows.explainer: Our judgment: the accounts list £8.7m of grants (note 7(a)) without what they bought. Soi Dog (£1.7m), Hope & Animal Trust (£1.3m), Dogstar (£0.75m), AR Sofia (£0.4m) and smaller groups run catch-neuter-vaccinate programmes (counted here, not in the rabies model); if about £2.5m of the grants paid for sterilisation at £150 to £400 each all-in (surgery, catching, kennelling, follow-up: our judgment), that is 6,000 to 17,000 operations paid for in full. 12,000, 4,000 to 30,000. These are the operations Dogs Trust's money paid for, so the neutering branch's attribution applies to WVS's 43,444 only in substance; it is applied to all, a small understatement.

rows.label: Dogs neutered by Dogs Trust Bosnia, 2025
rows.explainer: Dogs Trust Bosnia has neutered over 115,000 dogs since 2011 (p. 37), about 8,000 a year on average, but is in phased withdrawal: its 2025 grant was £1.1m against £2.0m in 2024 (p. 87) and much of it now trains local partners. Our judgment 2,500, 1,000 to 5,000.

rows.label: Neutering vouchers used in Ireland, 2025

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: 995 veterinary vouchers were used to help support owners with neutering and veterinary treatment

rows.explainer: 995 vouchers for neutering and treatment; we count half as neuterings, 200 to all 995.

rows.label: Neuterings in the year (WVS, overseas grants, Bosnia, Ireland)
rows.explainer: WVS's count, Ireland's vouchers, and our judgments for the grants and Bosnia. No UK neutering programme was reported for 2025.

rows.label: Neutering: share of sterilisations that are females
rows.explainer: Our judgment: catch-neuter programmes target bitches (and spay queens), but catch whatever they can; 60%, 40% to 80%. Males' sterilisation averts no births on its own in a population with spare males.

rows.label: Neutering: litters a breeding female has a year
rows.explainer: Our judgment: free-ranging bitches breed about once a year (some twice, some skip); 1, 0.7 to 1.5.

rows.label: Neutering: pups per litter at first count (West Bengal)

source.title: Paul et al. 2016, High early life mortality in free-ranging dogs is largely influenced by humans, Scientific Reports 6:19641
source.quote: 364 pups from 95 litters

rows.explainer: 364 pups in 95 litters = 3.83 a litter when first counted (some die before); 3 to 5 for other places and earlier deaths.

rows.label: Neutering: breeding years left to a sterilised animal
rows.explainer: Our judgment: free-roaming adults live a few years; animals sterilised as young adults have about 2 breeding years left, 1 to 4. Counted undiscounted within those years (short).

rows.label: Neutering: share of averted births not made up by other dogs
rows.explainer: Our judgment: where food and shelter hold a population, fewer births raise other pups' survival and immigration; half the averted births stay averted, 20% to 80%. Anchor: sustained programmes cut free-roaming numbers by a quarter to most over years (85% in Sarajevo with enforcement and rehoming, p. 37).

rows.label: Unowned animals' births averted per neutering
rows.explainer: Births a sterilisation averts, net of rebound: the share female × litters a year × pups a litter × remaining breeding years × the share not made up by other dogs breeding or surviving more.

rows.label: Neutering: share of free-ranging pups that die before reproductive age

source.title: Paul et al. 2016, High early life mortality in free-ranging dogs is largely influenced by humans, Scientific Reports 6:19641
source.quote: ~19% of the 364 pups from 95 observed litters surviving till the reproductive age

rows.explainer: 81% die before seven months in West Bengal; 70% to 90% for other places.

rows.label: Neutering: days of disabling pain in a pup's life that ends early
rows.explainer: Our judgment: pups die of disease (parvovirus, distemper), starvation, cold and road traffic (63% of deaths human-influenced, Paul et al.); a few days of severe illness or injury plus weeks of hunger at a hurtful level: 8 days of disabling pain, 2 to 25.

rows.label: Neutering: days of disabling pain in a surviving free-ranging dog's life
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a free-roaming adult lives a few years with mange, wounds, transmissible tumours, parasites and hunger at a hurtful level part of the time (0.1 a day for a month or two a year) and dies of injury or disease: 50 days, 15 to 150.

rows.label: Days of disabling pain in the life of an unowned animal that isn't born
rows.explainer: A birth averted spares either a pup's short life ending in death (most) or an adult's hard life on the street, weighted by Paul et al.'s survival.

rows.label: Neutering: the sterilised animal's own days of pain spared, net of surgery
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a bitch spared pregnancies and nursing in poor condition (about 3 days a litter, 60% females, 2 litters) gains about 3.6 days, against about 2 days of post-operative pain where analgesia is thin: net +1, −2 (painful surgery, few pregnancies avoided) to +4.

rows.label: Days of pain spared by neutering (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The births come about a year later, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Neutering: the sterilised animals' own days, before adjustments
Neutering: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.6, below the care branches' 0.7: births averted rest on a population judgment (rebound, breeding years) with only litter size and pup survival measured; 0.4 if rebound is stronger than we assume, 0.8 if close to right.

rows.label: Neutering: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Few other groups neuter in these places; governments in some. Our judgment 0.8, 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: Neutering: Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: WVS and the grantees work with partners and governments, and the grants pay part of each grantee's costs. Our judgment 0.6, 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Neutering: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Neutering: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Some animals are already sterile or past breeding; 0.9, 0.8 to 1.

rows.label: Neutering: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Dogs Trust counts the dogs but no controlled study measures how much less they suffer, so the effect is our judgment from the welfare literature.

rows.label: Neutering: all adjustments combined
Neutering: days of disabling pain spared
Dogs a year the 2025 import law can spare a smuggled or mutilated import
rows.explainer: The Animal Welfare (Import of Dogs, Cats and Ferrets) Act 2025, which Dogs Trust campaigned for over ten years, got Royal Assent on 2 December 2025 and lets the government ban importing dogs under six months, heavily pregnant or with cropped ears (GOV.UK, 2 December 2025, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/pet-smuggling-crackdown-with-new-law). Neither the government nor Dogs Trust publish how many dogs that covers; our judgment from the scale of commercial and smuggled puppy imports into Great Britain: 20,000 a year, 5,000 to 60,000.

rows.label: Policy: days of disabling pain spared per dog not imported that way
rows.explainer: Our judgment: early separation, long transport, disease (parvovirus) and mutilation; about 10 days of disabling pain, 2 to 40. The puppies bred to replace them at home are assumed to fare as UK-bred dogs.

rows.label: Policy: years until the bans are in force
rows.explainer: The government will now write secondary legislation (GOV.UK, 2 December 2025); our judgment two years, 1 to 4.

rows.label: Policy: years counted, discounted, after the wait
rows.explainer: A won reform counts the site's one number of years ($win_years_counted, docs/normalization.md 2.9), each discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Policy: 2025's share of the campaign's cost
rows.explainer: The win came at the end of a campaign of more than ten years; 2025's spending gets its share of it, not the whole (Convention 11, a past average's cost and wins from the same period). Our judgment 15%, 8% to 30%: the final year's parliamentary push cost more than an average year.

rows.label: Policy: all 2025 wins against the import Act alone
rows.explainer: Our judgment: Dogs Trust's campaigning also shaped the Renters' Rights Act (tenants able to keep pets, fewer dogs given up for housing), the Housing (Scotland) Act and the Dog Theft (Scotland) Bill (the report's 'four major legislative changes', PDF pages 26 and 30); together about 30% more than the import Act, 1 (little effect on dogs' days) to 2.

rows.label: Policy: days of pain spared before adjustments
Import law: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.7, as for the other judged effects, because the pain each import causes is our judgment, not measured; 0.5 if imported pups fare closer to home-bred ones, 0.9 if close to right.

rows.label: Import law: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: whether the law would have come anyway is in the years counted ($win_years_counted, the years the win brought the change forward), not here (Convention 5).

rows.label: Import law: Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: A coalition won it: the RSPCA, the BVA, Four Paws, Battersea, Blue Cross, the Kennel Club and the MPs who brought the bill. Dogs Trust led for years and is the only charity rehoming smuggled pups; our judgment of its share of the resources, 15%, 5% to 30%.

rows.label: Import law: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Import law: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Smuggling continues outside the law and enforcement at the border is thin: 0.6, 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Import law: counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): Dogs Trust counts the dogs but no controlled study measures how much less they suffer, so the effect is our judgment from the welfare literature.

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: Supported 323 people to move to safety

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by a survivor who leaves abuse, points a year
rows.explainer: Our judgment anchored on Pawłowska-Muc et al. 2023 (Frontiers in Public Health, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2023.1073612/full): 305 Polish women experiencing domestic violence scored 13.78 on the Satisfaction With Life Scale (5 to 35) against 21.04 for 305 who weren't, about 2.4 points on a 0-10 scale; cross-sectional, so part of the gap is other differences, and leaving recovers part of the rest within the first year: 0.8 points, 0.2 to 1.5.

rows.label: Share of survivors who would not have left without the dog's foster care
rows.explainer: The one counterfactual question for survivors: the share of the gain that wouldn't have happened without the dog's foster care, counting those who would have left later in proportion to the time gained. Anchor: Freedom exists because very few refuges take pets and survivors face 'an impossible choice: remain at risk or leave their dog behind' (p. 21); most survivors would still leave, many later. 25%, 10% to 50%.

rows.label: Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind Freedom's moves to safety
rows.explainer: Foster carers give their homes unpaid and domestic-abuse services, refuges and support workers do much of the work of each move; our judgment of Dogs Trust's share of the resources behind the part owed to the dog, 60%, 40% to 85% (the dogs' side of the scheme uses 0.7).

rows.label: Freedom: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Years the survivor's life-satisfaction gain lasts (persistence only)
rows.explainer: How long a gain once made persists, not when the survivor would otherwise have left (that is in freedom_credit): 1.5 years, 0.5 to 4, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Children who leave with each survivor
rows.explainer: Our judgment: many survivors leave with children; 0.8, 0.3 to 1.5, each at child_gain_share of the adult's gain.

rows.label: A child's gain as a share of the adult survivor's
rows.explainer: Our judgment: children exposed to domestic abuse gain from leaving, measured less directly; half the adult's gain, 25% to 100%.

rows.label: Owners helped by the behaviour services (excluding Dog School)
rows.explainer: Owners given behaviour advice (the line, coaching and clinical cases share owners with several dogs); Dog School owners are left out (puppy classes, mostly no problem).

source.title: Dogs Trust Annual Report 2025 (year to 31 December 2025)
source.quote: supported more than 9,500 owners with expert behaviour advice

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained a year by an owner whose dog's problem eases, points
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Reference class: caregiver burden in owners of animals with chronic or behavioural problems, which Spitznagel et al. (Veterinary Record 2017) found raised owners' stress and depression scores against owners of healthy animals; we put relief from a dog's daily separation distress or aggression at 0.1 points of life satisfaction a year, a tenth of the gap the site's sources give for moderate life strains, 0.03 to 0.3. Applies only to the owners whose problem eases (prev_owner_share_eased), for as long as the dog's improvement lasts (prev_years_better_life), discounted.

rows.label: Share of advised owners whose dog's problem eases
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the same third the prevention branch's per-dog effect assumes (prev_suffering_share_avoided): behaviour advice resolves or eases a problem in a minority of cases; 33%, 15% to 50%.

rows.label: Life satisfaction gained by a homeless owner whose dog is treated or who can keep it in accommodation, point-years
rows.explainer: Our judgment: for people experiencing homelessness a dog is often their main companion (p. 20); free vet care and dog-friendly services keep them together and lift a worry: 0.05 point-years per owner helped, 0 to 0.2. One owner per dog helped.

rows.label: WELLBYs for the children who leave with survivors
rows.formula: freedom_people_safe * freedom_children_per_survivor * child_gain_share * freedom_ls_gain * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, freedom_years_gain) * freedom_credit * freedom_attribution_share * people_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: A household spillover (normalization.md 2.16), weighed by the shared slider.

rows.label: People: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no study measures survivors' or owners' life satisfaction after Dogs Trust's help; the gains are our judgment.

rows.label: WELLBYs for people: Freedom survivors and their children, owners given behaviour advice, homeless owners
rows.formula: (freedom_people_safe * freedom_ls_gain * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, freedom_years_gain) * freedom_credit * freedom_attribution_share + prev_owners * prev_owner_share_eased * prev_owner_ls_gain * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, prev_years_better_life) * prev_counterfactual_adj * prev_attribution_share * prev_implementation_adj + homeless_vet_dogs * homeless_owner_ls_gain * sup_counterfactual_adj * sup_attribution_share * sup_implementation_adj) * people_missing_data_adj + wellbys_freedom_children
rows.explainer: People the work aims at (Freedom exists for survivors; prevention for dogs and owners living together; Together Through Homelessness for owners), so not a side effect, except the children (their own row, a spillover). Each gain is discounted over its years and carries its branch's counterfactual, credit and delivery; thin data (× people_missing_data_adj). Adopters' own life satisfaction is counted as 0: studies of pet ownership and wellbeing find no consistent effect.

rows.label: Free-roaming dog-years averted by neutering
Years a surviving free-roaming dog lives as an adult
rows.explainer: Our judgment: free-roaming adults live a few years; 3, 1 to 6.

rows.label: People bitten per free-roaming dog-year
rows.explainer: Our judgment: bite incidence of a few per thousand people a year where free-roaming dogs number about one per 10 to 20 people gives about 0.02 bites per dog-year, 0.005 to 0.06. Anchor: Dogs Trust Bosnia's 75% fall in reported bites alongside 85% fewer free-roaming dogs in Sarajevo (p. 37), bites moving with numbers.

rows.label: Healthy years lost per dog bite (injury, not rabies)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most bites are minor wounds healed in weeks (disability weight about 0.05 for a few weeks), some need surgery or leave scars, and each costs a course of post-exposure shots: 0.008 healthy years, 0.002 to 0.03. Rabies deaths are in the rabies model, not here.

rows.label: Healthy years from fewer dog bites, per dollar you give
rows.explainer: A side effect for people of fewer free-roaming dogs (normalization.md 2.16), weighed by the shared slider.

rows.label: Fewer dog bites, in chicken-equivalent pain days per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into this model's unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6).

rows.label: WELLBYs for people per dollar you give
WELLBYs for people, in chicken-equivalent pain days per dollar you give
rows.explainer: The bridge from WELLBYs into this model's unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): the headline multiplies the unit's conversion back, so the people's gain reaches healthy years through the WELLBY's own conversion.

rows.label: Dogs' share of the treatment and neutering days
rows.explainer: WVS and the grantees work mostly with dogs (Dogs Trust's money is for dogs), with cats and some working equines; our judgment 75%, 60% to 90%. The rest is counted on the cat's weight, which is the same stand-in (a pig's) as the dog's, so working equines are not undervalued against dogs.

rows.explainer: Every UK, Irish and policy branch is dogs; overseas treatment and neutering are dogs at intl_share_dog. Weighted by days spared.
